static.title: Gravitational-wave observing lab
static.note: A model of two compact objects spiralling together, and the strain a detector would record from it. Leading-order inspiral only: it stops before the merger, and the readout says where.

presets.label: Two black holes
presets.note: Thirty-six and twenty-nine solar masses at 410 megaparsecs — the scale of the first detection. The whole inspiral above 20 Hz lasts under a second.

presets.label: Two neutron stars
presets.note: Two stars of 1.4 solar masses at 40 megaparsecs. From 20 Hz this binary radiates for over two minutes, so the lab models the last eight seconds and says so.

presets.label: Neutron star and black hole
presets.note: A 1.4 solar-mass neutron star with a ten solar-mass black hole. Everything different about this signal follows from the masses: the model has no tides, no disruption and no post-merger to add.

samples.label: Does this radiate?
samples.value: Yes. Two lumps going round each other change the SHAPE of the mass distribution — its quadrupole — and a changing quadrupole is what radiates. The rings are a propagation illustration; the strain is what the model computes.

samples.label: The rings
samples.value: One crest per cycle of the wave, which is twice per orbit. Where each ring is comes from the model’s own emission history, so pausing holds them and seeking back shows the earlier pattern. Their speed across the screen is a display choice, not the speed of light to scale.

samples.label: Display amplification
samples.value: The strain picture is drawn 10,000 times larger than life. Display only — nothing computed changes, and the real number is in the readout above.

samples.label: What the two objects are
samples.value: Drawn as two black holes. The model did not decide that: a point-mass inspiral has two masses in it and no material at all, and the same equations would give this waveform whatever the objects were made of. At these masses nothing else is known that could be this compact, which is an astrophysical inference and not a result of this calculation.

samples.label: Does this radiate?
samples.value: Yes. Two lumps going round each other change the SHAPE of the mass distribution — its quadrupole — and a changing quadrupole is what radiates. The rings are a propagation illustration; the strain is what the model computes.

samples.label: The rings
samples.value: One crest per cycle of the wave, which is twice per orbit. Where each ring is comes from the model’s own emission history, so pausing holds them and seeking back shows the earlier pattern. Their speed across the screen is a display choice, not the speed of light to scale.

samples.label: The ring, right now
samples.value: h₊ = 5.72e-22, h× = -3.07e-23. Those are the two numbers the picture is drawn from — the fractional change in length along the two directions. Both are dimensionless.

samples.label: Polarization
samples.value: Circular. Both polarizations are present and equal, a quarter cycle apart, so the ring is an ellipse of fixed shape that ROTATES. It never passes through a circle — not once. Looking face-on at a circular orbit is what does this.

samples.label: What an L would read
samples.value: Along the horizontal arm the length changes by a fraction 2.86e-22; along the vertical arm, -2.86e-22. The instrument measures the DIFFERENCE, 5.72e-22 — which on LIGO’s four-kilometer arms is 2.29e-18 meters. That is why the shape is an L: two lengths compared against each other, not one length measured absolutely.

samples.label: What the two objects are
samples.value: Drawn as two black holes. The model did not decide that: a point-mass inspiral has two masses in it and no material at all, and the same equations would give this waveform whatever the objects were made of. At these masses nothing else is known that could be this compact, which is an astrophysical inference and not a result of this calculation.

static.title: Laboratorio de observación de ondas gravitacionales
static.note: Un modelo de dos objetos compactos que caen en espiral, y la deformación que registraría un detector. Solo espiral a orden principal: se detiene antes de la fusión, y la lectura dice dónde.

presets.label: Dos agujeros negros
presets.note: Treinta y seis y veintinueve masas solares a 410 megaparsecs: la escala de la primera detección. Toda la espiral por encima de 20 Hz dura menos de un segundo.

presets.label: Dos estrellas de neutrones
presets.note: Dos estrellas de 1,4 masas solares a 40 megaparsecs. Desde 20 Hz esta binaria radia más de dos minutos, así que el laboratorio modela los últimos ocho segundos y lo dice.

presets.label: Estrella de neutrones y agujero negro
presets.note: Una estrella de neutrones de 1,4 masas solares con un agujero negro de diez. Todo lo distinto de esta señal viene de las masas: el modelo no tiene mareas, ni disrupción, ni posfusión que añadir.

static.title: GW150914, as published
static.note: Measured strain from the two LIGO detectors, released with the discovery paper. The collaboration band-passed it to 35–350 Hz before publishing; nothing else has been done to it here.

presets.label: As published
presets.note: Both traces exactly as released. They do not look alike, and that is the starting point rather than a problem.

presets.label: Shifted and inverted
presets.note: Livingston moved 6.9 ms earlier and flipped in sign. Both are physical: the wave crossed the Earth, and the two detectors’ arms are turned relative to each other.

static.title: GW150914, tal como se publicó
static.note: Deformación medida por los dos detectores de LIGO, publicada con el artículo del descubrimiento. La colaboración la filtro en banda de 35 a 350 Hz antes de publicarla; aquí no se le ha hecho nada más.

presets.label: Tal como se publicó
presets.note: Ambas trazas exactamente como se publicaron. No se parecen, y ese es el punto de partida, no un problema.
